reviewer: single-reader (Claude Sonnet 5.5, this session), judged from the quote, its section, the article title and year, and the curator's question; the full papers were not read. Not independently reviewed.

scale.quote_supports_stance: yes | partly | no: does the quoted passage say what the attestation's stance (open or settled) claims about a facet
scale.fit_to_question: direct | partial: does that facet cover the curator's question as phrased

items.note: The quote (the 2022 article's own abstract conclusion; its title states the same finding) describes a stochastic fate switch inside a competence window, which speaks to the question's 'only some cells become endoderm'. One study's conclusion is labelled settled; whether the field treats it so is not in the quote, and the question as a whole (how the pattern becomes fates) is wider.

The quote asserts that elevated thyroid hormone and metabolism promote cardiomyocyte cycle exit and polyploidization, limiting regeneration. The cited 2025 article is a single zebrafish knockout study (title); the quote does not show that it settles the mammal-versus-zebrafish difference the question asks about.

The quote supports reduced regeneration with age, in 'both species'; the article title shows these are zebrafish and turquoise killifish, so the zebrafish age facet is supported by one 2023 study. The repeated-amputation part and 'under what conditions' of the question are not addressed by the quote.

The quote states that periodicity is unproven beyond the first billion steps and that a proof is needed. It matches the question. This is a mathematics prize problem on a blog announcement, sitting in a biology register; its attestation is not biology literature.

The quote supports the second half of the question (how and when veins acquire mural coverage is little known, in a 2021 review). The first half, what restricts recruitment to arteries, is not in the quote.
A 2015 commentary says how organ sizes stay proportionate 'remains mysterious'. It matches the question; it is an opinion in a perspective piece, as of 2015.

The quote says reconstruction of the gene regulatory network executing somite segmentation in the anterior presomitic mesoderm is 'not completely resolved' (2024 review). The named Tbx6, Mesp and Ripply network and the clock-to-boundary step are not in the quote, so it supports a nearby open area more than this specific question.

The quote states that it is unclear to what extent arterial and venous pole derivatives share a common progenitor pool in the early lateral plate mesoderm (2021 review). This closely matches the question.

The quote says the mechanisms of radial intercalation are 'not yet fully understood' and itself cites a 2010 review, inside a 2017 article, so the openness statement is dated to the 2010 literature. The question's second part (how much is a response to enveloping-layer expansion) is not in the quote.

The quote says the dating results remain compatible with a prolonged rediploidization process, which 'remains a viable mechanism' for teleost novelties (the 2024 article's title also says its dating is 'compatible with' delayed rediploidization). That is a statement of compatibility, not a statement that the causal question is unresolved, so a stance of 'open' is not supported by this quote.
The quote says the precise mechanism linking cell stretch to proliferation 'is not known' (2012 article). It matches the question; the openness is as of 2012 and later work was not checked.
The quote says how spines arose, and why fin ray structure differs in some species, 'remains to be fully understood' (2026 article). It matches the question.

The quote says a central organizing centre producing 'as-yet-undiscovered' morphogens has been proposed (citing an earlier reference). It matches the question's unknown source and signals; the organizing centre is a proposal, not a finding.

The quote says lineage tracing is needed to assess whether the cells indeed are stem cells, which supports the 'which are self-renewing' facet. The 2019 article is a single-cell sequencing study that itself proposes populations; the question's first half (which cells give rise to regenerated hair cells) is not addressed by the quote.
The quote calls both parts of the question 'open questions' (2023 article). It matches the question.
